Daniel Thrower has been jailed at Leeds Crown Court for three years for causing serious injury to two-year-old JJ Michalowski. The 34-year-old was sentenced after a head-on collision that left the toddler paralysed for life. Thrower, driving under the influence and on the wrong side of the road, was also banned from driving. The incident occurred in Hemsworth, West Yorkshire, shortly after JJ had taken his first steps upstairs.

The court heard that JJ's injuries are so severe he will never walk again and requires a ventilator while sleeping. His parents, Katy and Igor Michalowski, were present at the hearing, where they learned Thrower will serve a portion of his three-year sentence, but felt it was not enough for the crime.

On the evening of the crash, Thrower consumed approximately four beers before taking his girlfriend's car without permission. He had no valid insurance and his license had been revoked six years prior for a similar drink-driving offense. While driving on the A628 bypass in Hemsworth, Thrower collided head-on with a Peugeot 407 driven by Igor Michalowski, in which JJ and his sisters, Llacia and Leah, were passengers.

The family was on their way to drop Katy, 27, at her nursing home job. Michael Smith, prosecuting, stated that JJ sustained severe spinal cord injuries, resulting in paralysis from the trunk down. Doctors believe it is highly unlikely he will ever walk again and will require a wheelchair for daily activities.

In a victim impact statement, JJ's family expressed their devastation, stating they have been unable to cuddle him properly since the March 8 incident. They lamented that JJ has been robbed of a normal, happy childhood. Thrower, from Doncaster, South Yorkshire, was hospitalized after the crash but was reportedly uncooperative and had to be restrained. His defense lawyer cited a recent relationship breakdown and medication for depression as mitigating factors.

Judge Geoffrey Marson QC sentenced Thrower to three years for causing serious injury by dangerous driving and aggravated vehicle taking, emphasizing that Thrower knowingly drove without permission, insurance, or a valid license while unfit to drive. He acknowledged that the sentence could not measure the devastation caused to JJ's family.

Outside the court, JJ's family expressed their outrage and pain. Igor Michalowski stated that no sentence would be sufficient for the damage caused. JJ's grandmother, Lesley Liddle, condemned Thrower's actions, and his aunt, Lynne Clifford, called for stricter laws to protect innocent people. Thrower is disqualified from driving for three years and must complete an advanced driving course before reapplying for a license. JJ's family is raising funds for specialist equipment, including a joystick-controlled wheelchair, to aid his independence. Donations can be made via his Facebook page.

article_content: A New York man, Miguel Mejia-Ramos, 29, has been charged with the murder of his wife and their two young daughters after they were found stabbed to death. Mejia-Ramos allegedly claimed he killed the children because he lacked car seats to take them with him while fleeing. Mejia-Ramos was placed on suicide watch after his arraignment on Friday. Prosecutors stated that he told investigators he killed his children because of the absence of car seats, which he claimed prevented him from taking them as he attempted to flee. He was apprehended at a vehicle roadblock in Schulenburg, Texas, while trying to escape to Mexico. The victims, Deisy Garcia, 21, and her daughters, aged one and two, were found stabbed in their Queens home on January 18. Mejia-Ramos' attorney has not yet responded to requests for comment. He was arrested in Texas on Monday, en route to Mexico, after authorities tracked his cellphone. He agreed on Wednesday to return to New York. Deisy Garcia, 21, one-year-old Yoselin Mejia, and two-year-old Daniela Mejia were found dead in their bedrooms last Sunday. Authorities recovered five knives with apparent blood stains. According to the New York Daily News, Mejia-Ramos told police he attempted suicide after killing his family 'but couldn't do it.' After his arrest, Mejia-Ramos stated that he was looking through his wife's phone and Facebook page on Sunday night and became enraged upon seeing a photo of her with another man. He then stabbed Deisy Garcia, hugged and kissed his two young daughters, Daniela and Yoselin, before killing them as well. Mejia-Ramos was arrested earlier this week in La Grange, Texas, after activating his cellphone, which allowed authorities to track him. He was stopped by U.S. Marshals just before midnight on Monday while driving a car with New York State license plates and attempting to enter Mexico, where he was born, according to police sources. Four NYPD detectives went to Texas to interview Mejia-Ramos, and he agreed to return to New York on Wednesday. He is facing first-degree murder charges. Friends of Deisy Garcia described her as a quiet but happy person, and a good mother to her daughters. The victims were discovered dead in their apartment on Sunday night after friends noticed they hadn't attended church. Garcia's uncle discovered the scene at around 7pm on Sunday. All three had suffered multiple stab wounds, and two bloody knives were initially found in the rooms where the bodies were located, although authorities recovered five knives in total. A friend, Diana Villa, told the New York Post that Garcia was afraid of Ramos and had asked their local pastor for help, but she was scared of calling the police because she was an undocumented immigrant from Guatemala. Villa stated she had witnessed a violent argument between the couple at a recent baby shower after Ramos accused Garcia of not providing beer at the party, which was held at the church. Garcia's uncle discovered the bodies at their home in Queens, New York, in January. Neighbors said that the couple fought, and police had responded to domestic violence complaints previously. The home, located above a drug store, was cordoned off on Sunday night after the discovery. Police officers had visited the residence in response to domestic violence complaints against Ramos in November and May, but he was not arrested on either occasion. Garcia’s uncle, Ramon Chuc, 37, recalled finding the bodies with his two sons, ages 12 and 10, after they returned home from playing football outside. 'My 12-year-old son, Rene, went inside the room and saw my niece on the floor,' Chuc said. 'After that, I saw the two babies covered with a blanket. I took it off and saw them.' All three were pronounced dead at the scene with stab wounds to the chest. The apartment was cordoned off by police. ‘She was a quiet but happy person. She always had a smile on her face. She was a good mom,’ Mario Sanchez, 16, told the Daily News.

Neville Williams, 56, has been sentenced to ten years in prison for breaking into a teenage mother's home and raping her. The crime occurred on October 1, 1999, which was Williams' 42nd birthday. He boasted about it during the brutal assault. The victim, 19 at the time, was threatened by Williams, who said he would return and rape her again if she reported the incident to the police.

After enduring the ordeal, the terrified young woman fled her home in Birmingham and resettled elsewhere in the country to escape the painful memories. However, after 12 years of silence, she finally reported the crime to the police in November 2011, leading to an investigation and the subsequent search for her attacker.

Williams was tracked down after the victim recalled that he used the nickname 'Crunch'. Following his arrest in June of the previous year, the unemployed Williams denied the attack and faced trial earlier this year. The jury found him guilty based on evidence from a friend and the victim’s GP, who testified about the changes in her personality following the assault.

At Birmingham Crown Court, Neville Williams, from Smiths Wood, Solihull, West Midlands, received a 10-year prison sentence. He was also ordered to sign the sex offenders’ register for life and subjected to a restraining order to protect his victim. The victim expressed relief after the verdict, stating she was 'stuck for words' and 'so pleased.' She added, 'Knowing he’s locked away and other girls are safe is the best thing ever.'

Detective Chief Inspector Dean Young of West Midlands Police commended the woman for her courage and appealed to any other potential victims to come forward. He stated, 'She is a role model for countless other women who have been assaulted over the years and who have never felt able to tell police officers their story.' He also urged anyone who had been assaulted by Williams but felt unable to report it to contact the police, emphasizing that 'now is the time to seek help.'

article_content: As SVP of Professional Services at BairesDev, Damian manages the entire customer relations life-cycle, safeguarding the company’s operations. We are surrounded by technology so much that it's an intrinsic part of the human experience in the 21st century—unless you are purposely trying to live off the grid. Today, even non-techies constantly check their smartphones, order products online, stream media, engage on social media, look for addresses on map apps and find new food joints online. Because technology is so ubiquitous in our daily lives, it also has the potential to bring about change for the better. Leaders in every industry, not only in tech, understand that their role is more than just pursuing profit. It also encompasses harnessing the potential of technological innovations to drive social change. In this article, I will make a case for how leaders should see profit and purpose as a combined goal and how to leverage technology for social good. Gone are the days when a CEO was all about the bottom line. A new generation of C-suite executives is beginning to see their roles as a way of becoming change-makers. This leadership ethos is all about leveraging those assets for the broader good. They view technological innovation as a tool for societal benefit beyond the commercial realm. The impacts of these changes can be in bridging socioeconomic gaps, providing affordable education to underprivileged parts of society, reducing the carbon footprint and improving healthcare. Let's examine a few examples. Apps like ShareTheMeal enable users to donate to someone in need with a simple click. The United Nations World Food Programme delivers meals in Africa, Central America, Ukraine, the Middle East, Southeast Asia or wherever the user chooses. Platforms like Coursera and Domestika democratize education by offering cheaper alternatives to traditional colleges and can help professionals in other areas pivot to a different career later in life. My company has also worked on projects with companies with the mission of reducing the carbon footprint. One of our clients has a tech platform to give users easy access to clean energy. Their platform gives individuals greater control over what type of energy they support, how much it costs and how they pay. The platform also doubles as a marketplace for consumers and producers of solar energy. Another exciting project we developed was a first-of-its-kind online clinic to help women be in control of their health during the second half of their lives. Their team of doctors and coaches serves patients in all 50 U.S. states, improving the quality of healthcare options patients have access to. These examples were all born from leadership visions that extended beyond profit. For companies that already have an established business model but want to do more to increase their social empowerment, they must do the following: Integrate purpose into company DNA, foster collaboration, and invest in R&D for social solutions. Sustainable societal change takes time and commitment. That is why leaders must understand that while their vision is the guidance, the stakeholders—from employees to consumers—play a pivotal role in driving social change. Engaging with these groups, gathering feedback and ensuring tech solutions resonate with genuine societal needs will amplify the positive impact. One way to get all your team members on board is to involve them in decision-making and problem-solving. Providing adequate resources, support and tools to perform their work effectively is vital. It is also essential to encourage talent to pursue their professional goals by providing them with training, mentoring and career progression. For example, my company has the Giveback Program every year—an initiative that supports causes that promote STEM education and improved access to technology. We invite all our clients to participate in the endeavor, in which we donate on their behalf to one of three preselected nongovernmental organizations. This way, we involve our clients and our people in making a difference in the world. It seems that many leaders in the tech world are beginning to understand the intersection of profit and purpose and act accordingly. The digital age has equipped leaders with tools that, when used responsibly, can weave societal transformation into the fabric of their business models. The journey toward tech for social good is a collective one, where leaders serve as torchbearers, guiding their teams and stakeholders toward a future where technology doesn't just make life easier but also makes the world better. The question for every leader today is not whether they can drive profits through tech but how they can leverage that tech to leave an indelible mark on society.

article_content: The couple, Anne and Michael Harris, described by their niece as 'extraordinary' and possessing a great enthusiasm for life, were among the passengers on the ill-fated Air France Flight 447. Charlstie Laytin, their niece, expressed the family's hope that the Harrises would be remembered for their vibrant lives, not for their tragic end, during a telephone interview on Wednesday. The family is profoundly saddened by their loss. The Harrises were two of the three Americans aboard the flight, which crashed on Monday. The aircraft, carrying 228 individuals including passengers and crew, was traveling from Rio de Janeiro to Paris when it went down approximately four hours into its journey. The cause of the accident remains under investigation. As of Wednesday afternoon, an official list of the victims had not been released. Anne Harris's sister, Mary Miley, indicated that the Harrises resided in Rio de Janeiro. Michael Harris, aged 60, worked as a geologist in Rio de Janeiro for Devon Energy, a U.S.-based natural gas and oil producer, according to a company spokesperson. The couple was en route to Paris for a training seminar and a vacation, according to Miley. Laytin reminisced about the Harrises' positive outlook on life and her uncle's ability to bring laughter even on difficult days. She recalled a family gathering in Vermont a few summers prior, where they enjoyed wine, conversation, and laughter while sharing updates about their lives. The Harrises, she noted, were always interested in the activities of their nieces, nephews, and other family members. She cherishes that memory as their last family gathering. The family is hopeful that the investigation will soon reveal the cause of the crash. Laytin mentioned that the initial shock has begun to subside, and the reality of their loss is setting in, initiating the grieving process. The family is now focusing on supporting each other through this difficult time. The majority of the flight's passengers were from Brazil, France, and Germany, with the remaining victims representing 29 other countries. Ten individuals were employees of the French electrical equipment supplier CGED, as reported by Agence France-Presse. Nine of these employees had earned the trip to Rio through a sales competition, according to AFP. Laurent Bouveresse, CGED's chief executive, told AFP that the top sales representatives were rewarded with a four-day trip to Brazil. These employees were also allowed to bring a friend or partner, and an executive accompanied them, according to the news agency. CNN's attempts to contact CGED representatives were unsuccessful. Additionally, Julia Schmidt of Brazil and Alex Crolow of Germany, an engaged couple, were believed to be on the flight, according to their friend, Brian Buzby of Houston, Texas, who spoke with CNN affiliate KTRK. Buzby met the couple while they were students at Bucerius Law School in Germany, from which they graduated last August, KTRK reported. Buzby shared with KTRK that Alex was accompanying Julia to introduce her to his mother to announce their engagement. Buzby expressed his hope that they did not suffer and found solace in being together. He concluded by saying that they were his two best friends and he hoped Julia knew that he loved her.

article_content: Google has announced a new update for its AI chatbot, Bard, that allows users to ask the AI chatbot questions about YouTube videos and receive answers related to the video's content. 'We're taking the first steps in Bard's ability to understand YouTube videos,' Google wrote on Bard's update page. 'For example, if you're looking for videos on how to make olive oil cake, you can now also ask how many eggs the recipe in the first video requires,' Google explained. The company stated it expanded 'the YouTube Extension to understand some video content so you can have a richer conversation with Bard about it'. Before this update, the YouTube Extension for Bard could only be used to find specific videos. The update arrives two weeks after YouTube began experimenting with new generative AI capabilities, such as an AI conversational tool that answers queries about YouTube content and a feature that summarises topics in a video's comments. Meanwhile, Google has announced that Bard will be available for teens in most countries, with some safety measures in place. 'Teens in those countries who meet the minimum age requirement to manage their own Google Account will be able to access Bard in English, with more languages planned for the future,' said Tulsee Doshi, Head of Product, Responsible AI at Google. Before launching for teens, Google consulted with child safety and development experts to help shape its content policies and prioritize safety. The initial public offering (IPO) market is experiencing a significant bull wave. Three of the four IPOs—Tata Technologies, Flair Writing Industries, and Gandhar Oil Refinery—that opened on Wednesday were fully subscribed within hours. IndiGo is considering introducing a premium class of seats, along with hot food and a loyalty programme, by the end of 2024, as India’s largest airline aims to attract more business flyers and compete with Air India on international routes, according to sources. Creditors have withdrawn 26,518 insolvency cases involving defaults of approximately ₹9.33 lakh crore before their applications were admitted by the adjudicating authority since the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) came into effect.

Air Force Reserve Captain Jamie Brunette, whose family believes she was sexually assaulted while serving in Afghanistan, died by suicide using her handgun. Brunette, 30, from Tampa, Florida, was found dead on February 9 in the back of her locked sedan near her apartment by Tampa police. Authorities reported to the Tampa Tribune that she apparently died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound using her Smith & Wesson .380 handgun, which she had purchased about six months prior. The news of her death shocked her family. Brunette had left active duty after 11 years last June and joined the Air Force Reserve, and she had not shown any signs of being suicidal. She was also in the process of opening a new fitness business.

'She had so much going for her,' said Jackie Leverich, 40, Brunette's oldest sister. 'She was so full of hope, wonderment, passion, and excitement for life.' To the outside world, Brunette seemed happy. The week before her death, she posted photos of her studio under construction with the caption 'Doing work today!'. The studio was scheduled to open in a few weeks, and Brunette was a part-owner and instructor. However, Leverich believes that a traumatic incident occurred during her sister's deployment in Afghanistan. The family noticed a change in Brunette when she returned for her sister's wedding.

'She seemed upbeat,' Leverich said, 'but she wasn't really giving us a whole lot of detail about life and what was going on.' Leverich suspects that her sister was sexually assaulted in Afghanistan, though she lacks definitive proof. 'I suspect she was assaulted, and she didn't feel comfortable reporting it for some reason and internalized the incident so she could finish her deployment, which she did with flying colors,' Leverich stated. 'It's not anything she told me, just from talking with all her friends this past week, and piecing those things together. 'I am female active duty, 18 years in the Coast Guard. I am well aware of those issues, and that's my gut feeling.' The following year, Brunette left active duty and joined the Air Force Reserve.

Air Force Lt. Col. Kurt Spranger, her business partner, told the Tampa Tribune: 'I do not know the detail, but unequivocally I can say, yes, something happened, something that should never happen to a human,' Spranger said. 'Something happened and it was why she wanted to get out, so she wouldn't have to deploy again.' He mentioned that Brunette had ended a relationship with her boyfriend two weeks before her death, but she did not appear outwardly unhappy and remained professional.

According to the Hillsborough County medical examiner's initial report, Brunette had a 'long tobacco and alcohol abuse history' and was experiencing depression and anxiety. Her roommate reported that Brunette had confided in her about seeking treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder from the VA and had been struggling with depression. The VA could not comment due to privacy regulations.

An online memorial page has received numerous comments. One user wrote: 'She was a wonderful, bright, positive, professional, Contingency Contracting Officer and Airmen. She was so young and so full of life, and I feel great sadness from the squadron that loved her very much.' Another user wrote: 'I recently met Jamie at Orange Theory in Largo. I was so impressed while talking to her - articulate, respectful, courteous, and interesting. She was full of life and excited about getting her business up and running.'

MailOnline has contacted the US Air Force for comment.

To speak to a trained counselor, call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1800 273 8255.

article_content: Alexian Lien, who was dragged from his SUV and beaten by a group of motorcyclists after a chase on a Manhattan highway, has filed a legal notice indicating his intent to sue New York City over the attack. Prosecutors allege that an off-duty police detective was reportedly among the bikers who pursued and assaulted Lien following a confrontation on the West Side Highway. (Source: To be verified). The September assault was recorded by one of the bikers and subsequently posted online. Lien sustained injuries requiring stitches after being attacked by the bikers in New York. He hit some of the bikers in an attempt to escape, but they caught up to him and beat him. He is now suing the city over the attack. According to reports, Lien filed a formal 'notice of claim' against the city in December, accusing the police department of inadequate officer training. (Date and details: To be verified). A spokeswoman for the city's Legal Department stated that they would defend the claim if it proceeds to a full lawsuit. Lien's notice claims that 'a vicious and unruly mob of motorcycle riders attacked and assaulted' him and 'vandalized his motor vehicle' by smashing the rear window near where his toddler was sitting. Video footage reportedly shows an individual, identified in some reports as an undercover detective, breaking one of the windows. (Status as 'undercover': To be verified). The individual pleaded not guilty to assault charges in November. Lien asserts that the NYPD was negligent in failing to properly hire and train its officers. The incident occurred when Alexian Lien, driving a Range Rover, reportedly panicked and hit some of the bikers while attempting to escape to protect his wife and child. Jeremiah Mieses is believed to have been hit. Christopher Cruz is pictured before being rear-ended by Alexian Lien, which allegedly initiated the chase. Cruz has been arrested for reckless driving. The Police Department identified Braszczok, Rodriguez, and two other officers as being involved with the biker group. Rodriguez, an Internal Affairs officer, stated he was 'nowhere near the scene' of the violence but admitted to riding with the bikers. (Source: To be verified). Eleven bikers have been arrested in connection with the SUV incident. Lien, 33, was driving the black SUV near 125th Street in Harlem when he was surrounded by the group of bikers. They pursued him for 50 blocks up the West Side Highway to the 178th Street exit, where he was pulled from his car while his wife and daughter watched him being attacked. Police have stated that the bikers were allegedly attempting to slow Lien down to take control of the highway. (Source: To be verified). Sources claim the motorcyclists had blocked off some of the West Side Highway's entrances to prevent other vehicles from entering the road near West 125th Street. Reportedly, Alexian Lien panicked, hitting the bike in front with his Range Rover, which initiated the videotaped chase that led to his beating. One video shows bikes performing stunts in the streets. Sources indicated that Cruz's driving instigated the chase, as Lien rear-ended him. They also said the riders initially tried to slow Lien down to get in front of him and take over the West Side Highway. (Multiple sources needed for verification). Cruz, who is not believed to be among the bikers who followed Lien, was briefly hospitalized for minor injuries, including lower back pain, according to authorities. Lien, a Columbia University graduate, was treated at Columbia University Medical Center and received stitches. The bikers had been riding alongside the Range Rover before the incident, and Christopher Cruz braked suddenly. Within minutes, the group of bikers surrounded the vehicle with the family inside. According to a police spokesman, Lien recalled that a large number of motorcyclists were driving 'erratically' and he 'accidentally collided with one'. Footage shows one motorcyclist braking abruptly in front of the car, appearing to be bumped. He pulled over, but some bikers allegedly began to damage the vehicle. The NYPD spokesman told MailOnline that Lien drove off 'to avoid an impending assault'. Video footage shows the Range Rover accelerating, knocking over bikes and motorcyclists. The bikers then pursued the vehicle for several minutes, sometimes getting very close and intimidating the driver. Eventually, the bikers surrounded the vehicle, blocking its path. A biker dismounted and attempted to open the door, but the SUV accelerated again, knocking down at least one more motorcyclist. The family was eventually stopped in Manhattan traffic, at which point bikers immediately ran to attack the vehicle, smashing the driver's window with a helmet and attempting to smash the rear door window where the child was sitting. The driver then accelerated away, knocking down bikers in his path. When they came to a standstill in heavy traffic, a biker jumped off and attacked the vehicle, smashing the driver's window with his helmet.

article_content: Maryland has become the 18th U.S. state to abolish the death penalty after Governor Martin O'Malley signed a bill outlawing capital punishment in the state. O'Malley, a Democrat mentioned as a potential presidential candidate in 2016, had pledged to sign the bill, which the Democrat-controlled legislature passed in March. The law replaces capital punishment with a sentence of life without parole. 'With the legislation signed today, Maryland has effectively eliminated a policy that is proven not to work,' O'Malley's office said in a statement. The governor's office stated that the death penalty does not deter crime, cannot be administered without racial bias, and costs three times as much as life without parole. The statement added that a mistake cannot be reversed if an innocent person is put to death. Five other states—Connecticut, Illinois, New Mexico, New York, and New Jersey—have repealed capital punishment since 2007, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. 'That's six states in six years,' said Richard Dieter, the Center's executive director. Since Maryland reinstated the death penalty in 1978, 58 people have been sentenced to death in the state, but only five sentences have been carried out. Maryland has five men on death row, and its last execution took place in 2005. The number of U.S. executions has fallen from a peak of 98 in 1999 to 43 each in 2011 and 2012, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. The pace has slowed even more in 2013, with 10 executions so far this year. Texas has by far the highest number of executions since the U.S. Supreme Court restored the death penalty in 1976, with 496, according to the center. Virginia follows with 110. Dieter said the death penalty had fallen out of favor largely because lawmakers and the public increasingly feared that innocent people could be executed. He noted that lengthy legal appeals made it an expensive proposition, adding, 'It all adds up (as) a costly and rarely used punishment.' Kent Scheidegger, a death penalty advocate and legal director of the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation in Sacramento, California, said some crimes, such as the bombings at the Boston Marathon, justified the punishment. 'The main reason is just simple justice,' said Scheidegger. 'There are some crimes where a lesser penalty is insufficient.' He added that capital punishment could act as a deterrent to crime when correctly applied. Multiple states had bills pending to abolish the death penalty, but it was unclear which might be the next to overturn it, Dieter said. Among possible contenders is Nebraska, where the single-chamber legislature turned down a repeal bill in March by one vote. The Florida Senate this week moved to speed up executions by sending to Governor Rick Scott reforms designed to keep condemned inmates from spending decades on death row. O'Malley, a former Baltimore mayor and prosecutor, succeeded in his second attempt since 2009 to overturn capital punishment. It is part of a series of socially liberal measures he has championed in Maryland, including gun control, same-sex marriage, and allowing undocumented immigrants to pay in-state tuition at state colleges. Ted Sheckels, a political analyst at Virginia's Randolph-Macon College, said O'Malley's progressive stance, including the death penalty repeal, could help him if he decides to run for president in 2016. 'There have been a number of things that position him on the liberal side of things, which in a Democratic primary is where you want to be,' he said.

article_content:
Gary Sheehy deceived Lee Mackie, a Royal Marine's mother, persuading her to invest £4,350, proceeds from her son Jason's life insurance after he was killed by an improvised explosive device in Afghanistan, into his struggling camping equipment business. Sheehy promised she would double her money within two years. Although the business existed, Sheehy, 50, misrepresented its success, falsely claiming thousands of orders were pending when it was failing. After months of unanswered calls and excuses, Ms. Mackie, 58, reported Sheehy, her neighbor’s boyfriend, to the police.

Sheehy avoided immediate imprisonment, receiving a nine-month prison sentence suspended for two years. He was ordered to repay £2,000 after admitting fraud at an earlier hearing. Oxford Crown Court heard that Ms. Mackie received approximately £60,000 in life insurance after her 21-year-old son Jason, of the 3rd Armoured Support Group, died in 2009. Sheehy befriended her because his partner was her next-door neighbor in Bampton, Oxfordshire.

Prosecutor Patrick Moran told the court, 'He abused that friendship and the trust placed in him by Ms. Mackie at a vulnerable time.' In June 2010, Ms. Mackie gave Sheehy £10,000 to start a motor vehicle sales business, which failed, though no criminal charges were filed for that. In October, he asked for another £3,500 for the camping equipment firm, claiming equipment was in production and 140,000 units were ordered. 'In fact, the device was never in production, and no orders were placed,' Mr. Moran stated. A few months later, Sheehy requested another £850, purportedly to repay a customer in York who received faulty equipment.

Mr. Moran argued that Sheehy was willing to 'behave recklessly' with other people’s money. Defense lawyer Peter De Feu claimed Sheehy didn't intend to defraud Ms. Mackie, saying, 'It is a business that, if it had worked, would have made her a lot of money. He may not have been entirely open with Ms. Mackie about how badly it failed. He was desperately trying to keep what he thought was a brilliant idea alive and misled her.'

The court heard that Sheehy lives with two women in separate homes, one of whom he has two children with, ages three and eight months, and he financially supports both households. Mr. De Feu said Sheehy started a new car trading business and was 'absolutely determined' to repay Ms. Mackie, including the £10,000 from the vehicle business. He argued that imprisonment would have 'devastating effects' given Sheehy's responsibilities.

Sheehy, wearing a grey suit, pink shirt, and purple tie, showed no emotion as the case details were presented. Judge Ian Pringle, sentencing Sheehy, said, 'You can imagine the effect that has had on her. She feels betrayed by your actions.' However, the judge believed the act was 'totally out of character' for Sheehy, leading to a more lenient sentence. Judge Pringle warned that if Sheehy re-offends, the nine-month sentence would be fully implemented.

After the hearing, Ms. Mackie expressed no surprise at Sheehy avoiding immediate imprisonment. 'I still struggle to put it into words - it was the most devastating thing that has ever happened in my life. People say time makes it better, but it doesn’t,' she said of her son's death. 'Of course I think he should have gone to prison, but I didn’t think it was going to happen. To have got him put inside would have been the cherry on top of the cake.'

Ms. Mackie was pleased Sheehy would do 120 hours of unpaid work but doubted he'd repay the £4,350 and £10,000. 'He’s not a con artist for nothing,' Ms. Mackie said. 'He can talk himself out of anything.' Reflecting on the fraud, Ms. Mackie said, 'I was furious, because of where the money had come from. I had this huge guilt that I had blown this money which cost my child his life. I suddenly got this huge anxiety and guilt about using the money and being taken for a ride. I was so scared I couldn’t even tell my other two sons. I am not a stupid person, but because I was so vulnerable I allowed this man to con me into giving it to him.'

La Sra. Mackie se alegró de que Sheehy hiciera 120 horas de servicios comunitarios, pero dudaba de que devolviera las £4,350 y £10,000. 'No es un estafador por nada', dijo la Sra. Mackie. Me sentía muy culpable de haber despilfarrado este dinero que le costó la vida a mi hijo. De repente sentí una gran ansiedad y culpa por usar el dinero y por haber sido engañada. article_content: Judge Esther Salas of the U.S. District Court sentenced Teresa Giudice to 15 months in federal prison, while her husband, Joe Giudice, received a 41-month sentence. Both were also ordered to each pay $414,588 in restitution. Following their prison terms, the couple will each serve two years of probation. These sentences came close to the maximum possible after they pleaded guilty earlier in the year to conspiracy involving mail and wire fraud, as well as three types of bankruptcy fraud. Before her sentencing, Teresa tearfully stated, 'I am more sorry than anyone will ever know,' and told the judge, 'I will make this right.' Teresa, age 42, is scheduled to begin her prison sentence on January 5. Joe will report to prison after Teresa completes her sentence, ensuring that one parent is always available for their four daughters. Assistant U.S. Attorney Jonathan W. Romankow had suggested a 21-month sentence for Teresa, stating that she had disrespected the court and was now seeking sympathy. Jack Barbosa, who was present in the courtroom, reported Romankow's statement. Judge Salas indicated that the law applies equally to everyone and that actions have consequences. She deemed imprisonment necessary, acknowledging she briefly considered probation for Teresa, but ultimately felt Teresa lacked respect for the law. Joe, age 43, also admitted guilt to not filing a tax return for 2004 and acknowledged failing to report approximately $1 million in income between 2004 and 2008. He received a 12-month sentence for this, which will run simultaneously with his 41-month sentence. With good behavior, Teresa could be released in as little as 12 months. U.S. Attorney for New Jersey, Paul Fishman, described the sentences as 'fair, appropriate and reasonable.' Early in the day, Judge Salas reprimanded the couple for not disclosing purchases such as recreational vehicles, home furnishings, cars, and construction equipment. The judge highlighted inconsistencies and omissions in their financial disclosures, noting that they claimed only $25,000 worth of furniture in their $3 million home, suggesting the production company provided furnishings. However, they had a $1 million insurance policy on the home. In 2009 bankruptcy filings, they declared $60,000 in assets in their home, contradicting their more recent claims. According to NJ.com, Judge Salas stated that they had a duty to be transparent, which she felt they had not fulfilled. A reporter from the Star-Ledger reported that the judge found their omissions and inconsistencies concerning. Joe's lawyer attributed these issues to his grief over his father's death in June, stating it had significantly affected him. Joe also read a statement expressing humiliation and taking responsibility for his actions, promising to improve. The couple accepted a plea deal in March, confessing to concealing assets from bankruptcy creditors and submitting fraudulent loan applications to obtain approximately $5 million in mortgages and construction loans. Earlier in the week, a bankruptcy judge rejected their request to discharge over $13 million in debt. Judge Salas mentioned that immigration services would postpone Joe's deportation case until after his prison term. Joe's lawyers stated he came to the U.S. from Italy as an infant and was unaware of his lack of citizenship. Radar Online reported that his lawyers advised him to prepare for deportation after serving his sentence. The judge also suggested Joe participate in an alcohol program, following his lawyer's revelation of Joe's drinking problem and recommendation for rehab. Their four daughters will not be left without a parent, as Teresa and Joe will serve their sentences at different times. Teresa told the judge her daughters are her life and that she doesn't care about the TV show. NBCUniversal, which owns Bravo, the network airing Real Housewives, declined to comment on the Giudices' status with the show.

A ambos también se les ordenó pagar individualmente $414,588 en restitución. Después de cumplir sus condenas, la pareja estará bajo libertad condicional por dos años cada uno. Estas sentencias estuvieron cerca del máximo posible tras declararse culpables a principios de año de conspiración para cometer fraude postal y electrónico, además de tres tipos de fraude de bancarrota. Antes de la lectura de la sentencia, Teresa declaró entre lágrimas: 'Lo siento más de lo que nadie jamás sabrá' y le aseguró al juez: 'Voy a enmendar esto'. Teresa, de 42 años, tiene previsto ingresar en prisión el 5 de enero. Joe lo hará una vez que Teresa termine su condena, para garantizar que una figura paterna/materna esté siempre presente para sus cuatro hijas. El fiscal federal adjunto Jonathan W. Romankow había sugerido una pena de 21 meses para Teresa, argumentando que había irrespetado al tribunal y ahora buscaba lástima. Jack Barbosa, presente en la sala, fue quien informó de la declaración de Romankow. La jueza Salas señaló que la ley se aplica por igual a todos y que los actos tienen consecuencias. Consideró que el encarcelamiento era necesario, reconociendo que barajó brevemente la posibilidad de la libertad condicional para Teresa, pero finalmente creyó que Teresa carecía de respeto por la ley. Joe, de 43 años, también se declaró culpable de no presentar la declaración de impuestos correspondiente a 2004 y admitió no haber declarado ingresos por valor de aproximadamente un millón de dólares entre 2004 y 2008. Recibió una pena de 12 meses por esto, que se ejecutará de forma simultánea con la pena de 41 meses. Con buen comportamiento, Teresa podría salir en libertad en tan solo 12 meses. El fiscal general de Nueva Jersey, Paul Fishman, calificó las sentencias como 'justas, apropiadas y razonables'. A primera hora del día, la jueza Salas amonestó a la pareja por no revelar compras como vehículos recreativos, mobiliario para el hogar, coches y equipos de construcción. La jueza resaltó las incongruencias y omisiones en sus declaraciones financieras, haciendo notar que afirmaban tener solo 25.000 dólares en mobiliario en su casa de 3 millones de dólares, dando a entender que la productora les proporcionaba los muebles. Sin embargo, tenían una póliza de seguro del hogar de 1 millón de dólares. En las declaraciones de quiebra de 2009, declararon activos por valor de 60.000 dólares en su casa, contradiciendo sus afirmaciones más recientes. Según NJ.com, la jueza Salas declaró que tenían la obligación de ser transparentes, obligación que, en su opinión, no habían cumplido. Un periodista del Star-Ledger informó de que a la jueza le resultaban preocupantes sus omisiones e incongruencias. El abogado de Joe achacó estos problemas al duelo por la muerte de su padre en junio, asegurando que le había afectado mucho. Joe también leyó un comunicado en el que expresaba su humillación, asumía la responsabilidad de sus actos y prometía mejorar. La pareja aceptó un acuerdo con la fiscalía en marzo, confesando haber ocultado activos a los acreedores en el proceso de bancarrota y haber presentado solicitudes de préstamo fraudulentas para obtener unos 5 millones de dólares en hipotecas y préstamos para construcción. A principios de esa semana, un juez de quiebras desestimó su petición de exoneración de deudas por valor de más de 13 millones de dólares. La jueza Salas mencionó que los servicios de inmigración pospondrían la tramitación del caso de deportación de Joe hasta después de que cumpla su condena. Los abogados de Joe declararon que llegó a Estados Unidos desde Italia siendo un bebé y que desconocía que no tenía la nacionalidad estadounidense. Radar Online informó de que sus abogados le aconsejaron que se preparara para su deportación una vez cumplida su condena. La jueza también aconsejó a Joe que participara en un programa de tratamiento del alcoholismo, tras la revelación por parte de su abogado de que Joe tenía problemas con la bebida y la recomendación de que se sometiera a rehabilitación. Sus cuatro hijas no se quedarán sin un progenitor, ya que Teresa y Joe cumplirán sus condenas en momentos diferentes. Teresa le dijo a la jueza que sus hijas son su vida y que no le importa el programa de televisión. NBCUniversal, propietaria de Bravo, la cadena que emite Real Housewives, declinó hacer comentarios sobre la situación de los Giudice en el programa.

article_content: What do you do when your 10-year-old son wakes up in the middle of the night screaming, 'There's a 'roo in my room!'? Beat Ettlin wrestled a kangaroo out of his house near Canberra after it crashed through a window. If you're Beat Ettlin, you subdue the marsupial, possibly with a headlock, drag it down your hallway, and toss it out the front door. Ettlin and his family were woken early Sunday when a 6-foot-tall kangaroo crashed through a window, landed on their bed, and thrashed around their house in the suburb of Garran, south of Canberra, Australia. 'At first, he (my husband) thought it was a lunatic ninja,' said Ettlin's wife, Verity Beman. 'It leaped through the window, like a martial-arts figure. It was very Jackie Chan-esque.' The family's one-story house is in a suburb adjacent to a kangaroo reserve. About 2 a.m. Sunday, their dog began barking furiously, possibly at possums, they thought. The family had grown accustomed to possums scampering across their roof every night since they moved in three weeks prior. Moments later, the window was smashed, and a black figure landed on their bed. Ettlin, after gathering his wits, exclaimed, 'It's OK. It's only a kangaroo,' Beman recalled. 'I was cowered under the quilt, thinking, 'No, it's not OK,' she said. The kangaroo jumped on top of the blanket that Beman and her 9-year-old daughter were hiding under. It then leaped onto the nightstand, punched holes in the furniture, and left blood stains on the wall as it bounced into their son's room. 'That's when his male instinct kicked in,' Beman said of her husband. After putting the 90-pound creature in a chokehold, Ettlin kept it low to the ground and pulled it toward the front door. He knew that kangaroos primarily use their hind legs for strength, Beman said. 'He held it by one arm. He opened the front door with the other, then the screen door,' she said. 'It bounced across our veranda and away.' Ettlin is a chef, originally from the Swiss city of Stans. Beman thinks an Australian might have approached the situation with more caution. 'They would be fully aware of the risk,' she said. With the house in shambles -- blood and shattered glass everywhere -- Ettlin stood surveying the damage in his shredded underpants. Scratch marks ran down his leg, but otherwise he was fine. 'I kept marveling at what he did,' Beman said. 'I called him my hero. My hero in Bonds undies.'

Luego saltó sobre la mesita de noche, hizo agujeros en los muebles y dejó manchas de sangre en la pared mientras saltaba hacia la habitación de su hijo. 'Ahí es cuando su instinto masculino se activó', dijo Beman sobre su esposo. article_content: Lord Leveson suggests that Ofcom should ‘verify’ a fresh, independent press regulator and serve as a ‘backup’ for those newspapers that choose not to participate. This plan could mean one of New Labour's prominent organizations would be ultimately in charge of how the press is regulated, according to Lord Leveson’s report. The judge argued his ideas wouldn’t mean the government is regulating newspapers, but laws are needed to make it happen. However, both David Cameron and Nick Clegg have voiced worries about the idea of changing the law to allow Ofcom to oversee the verification of this new independent regulatory group. The report proposes that the new organization could fine newspapers up to £1 million and demand they issue apologies on their front pages. The Prime Minister said he generally agrees with Lord Leveson’s suggestions but doesn't support creating new laws to enforce them. Lord Leveson explained his suggested new body – meant to replace the current Press Complaints Commission – would encourage good journalism and safeguard individual rights. According to the judge's plans, most members of the new body's board must be independent from the media industry; sitting editors, MPs, and ministers wouldn't be allowed on the board. A separate independent group – which might include an editor – would choose the board members and chairman; this group would be checked every two years by Ofcom to ensure its independence. Since Ofcom is a government-linked body, and its chief executive is chosen by ministers, some have concerns about whether the process is truly independent from the government. While David Cameron and Nick Clegg have different views on the Leveson report overall, they both disagree with involving Ofcom in press regulation. New legislation would be necessary for the new regulatory body to be legally recognized and for Ofcom to oversee its independence and effectiveness. Key proposals in the Leveson report include Ofcom acting as a backup regulator for newspapers not participating in the new scheme. Lord Leveson’s plan includes an arbitration process for resolving complaints between newspapers and the public; signing up would limit legal costs if disputes go to court, but this needs a change in the law. Lord Leveson also wants a law that 'legally obligates the Government to protect press freedom for the first time'. The idea of Ofcom being involved in press regulation has become a controversial part of the plan. Mr. Cameron cautioned that Ofcom is a strong regulatory body, and efforts should be made to reduce power concentrations rather than increase them. Ofcom was established in 2003 by Tony Blair. David Cameron stated in 2009 that 'Ofcom, as we know it, will cease to exist' if he became Prime Minister, as part of his crackdown on such organizations. Ed Richards, the current chief executive of Ofcom (appointed in 2006), formerly advised Mr. Blair on media matters and can hold the position indefinitely, as there isn’t a fixed term. Lord Justice Leveson insisted this shouldn't be seen as government regulation of the press; he describes it as independent regulation organized by the press, verified to ensure independence and effectiveness, allowing publishers to benefit from membership. Government-linked Ofcom, created by Tony Blair and headed by former New Labour advisor Ed Richards, is seen by critics as unable to impartially oversee press regulation due to the ministerial appointment of its boss. Mr. Clegg, while supportive of much of the Leveson plan, questions whether Ofcom is the right entity for this new, light touch role with print media, given its focus on broadcast media. Tory MP Philip Davies fears Ofcom would have excessive power, arguing these important decisions shouldn’t be handed over to an unelected and unaccountable body; he also believes the government shouldn't threaten legislation or regulation unless specific steps are taken by the press.

article_content: Nashville, Tennessee (CNN) -- Moses Chol enters a van, rubs his hands together, and signals for quiet. Addressing the passengers, his face breaks into a grin, teeth gleaming in the morning light. 'Today, we say goodbye to the north,' he announces, as young men and women cheer, visible through woolen scarves and hats. Chol is among approximately 70 Southern Sudanese gathered on a cold morning in a church parking lot in Clarkston, Georgia, a metro Atlanta area known for its refugee population. The group is traveling to Nashville to vote in a referendum that could divide Sudan into two: the north and the south. Several million people in Southern Sudan are voting this week in a historic referendum on whether to declare independence from the Khartoum-based government. About 55,000 Southern Sudanese are voting in the United States and seven other countries. Chol leads a convoy of over a dozen cars. As it leaves the parking lot, some passengers sing a song by former guerrilla fighters who now lead the government and army of semi-autonomous Southern Sudan. 'We will never surrender; we will keep fighting until we get what we want,' they sing in Arabic. At the song's conclusion, they pump their fists and chant: 'Yes to separation!' The referendum is part of the 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement that helped end two decades of civil war, which resulted in approximately 2 million deaths. The war pitted a government dominated by Arab Muslims in northern Sudan against black Christians or animists in the south. For Chol, the referendum feels like reparation. He's one of the Lost Boys: a generation of children who fled the civil war and are now scattered across continents. The United States resettled nearly 4,000 of them around a decade ago. The men, now mostly in their 20s and 30s, have spent the past decade rebuilding their lives. The war forced Chol and others to trek hundreds of miles through deserts and swamps, evading lions and other animals, during their journeys to neighboring countries. Once there, they lived in refugee camps for years. Chol, 32, says he has dreamed of this referendum for years. 'It's time for them to hear our voices, for us to revolt against all the pain we suffered,' the graduate student says. 'A lot of people have died for this day. ... I don't care what government comes after this. No government will be worse than what we have.' His voice trails off as he pauses and stares into space. 'Passing this referendum means my father did not die in vain. It means our children will not live scarred lives. ... We will be the last 'Lost Boys' Sudan will ever see.' The conflict scarred a generation in remote Southern Sudan, which is about the size of Texas but has limited paved roads. Through the years, hundreds of thousands of Sudanese fled the south to escape fighting and famine. Approximately 80 percent of Sudan's oil reserves are located in the south, another source of conflict. Although the north has developed more, the south has remained largely unchanged, according to Chol. 'This north claims they want to be one nation,' he says. 'How can we be when they have schools and clean water, and their children are not dying of preventable diseases? In the south, people still drink stagnant water. They have nothing.' Passengers add to the list of grievances with the north. Some cite the north's attempts to impose Sharia, or Islamic law, on non-Muslims -- a key reason the nation erupted in civil war in 1983. Sharia remains the law in northern Sudan. 'You see my hair. It would get me in trouble in the north because of Sharia law,' says Grace Ajawin, a bakery employee, pointing to her red cornrows. 'I want my children to walk out of the house without being forced to cover their hair, to wear what they want, to go to church without being forced to convert to Islam.' Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir has warned that he will tighten the application of Sharia in northern Sudan if Southern Sudan votes for independence. Everyone in the vans believes that the south will secede from the north. Any attempt to suggest a different outcome is dismissed. Ajawin is admonished when she says she will 'never' go back to Sudan if al-Bashir does not honor a vote to split. 'How can (al-Bashir) not honor the vote when the whole world is watching?' Marko Ayii, 25, retorts. 'You need to stop your negative thinking.' Chol says he will return home if Southern Sudan is reborn as a new nation. 'When I graduate, I'll thank the Americans for being kind to us, and go help my people,' he says. After about four hours, the convoy arrives at the Lost Boys Center, a one-story red brick building just south of the office towers of downtown Nashville. The center is one of eight polling stations across the United States that will be open until Saturday. More than 900 Southern Sudanese are registered to vote there, poll officials report. Other centers are located in Boston; Chicago; Dallas; Omaha, Nebraska; Phoenix; Seattle; and Washington. The vote is being organized by the Southern Sudan Referendum Commission. Outside the Nashville center, a crowd awaits. Some are dancing while others wave American and Southern Sudan flags. At the front of the line, Malual Machop, 42, of Nashville, waits to vote, weeping quietly. 'My crying is not for sadness; it's for happiness,' he says. 'I never knew I would vote for this separation in my lifetime. We have been slaves for so long. We are now being liberated.' Outside, Ngong Aguek, 42, a musician from Southern Sudan who traveled from Orlando to vote, is tearing up his Sudanese passport. The crowd claps and cheers as the pages scatter in the windy, wintry air. 'This passport has enslaved me for so long,' he says. 'It has treated me like a second-class citizen, destroyed my dignity, and killed and separated my family.' The musician says he has been targeted by the northern government for criticizing it. 'But (the truth) needs to be told, regardless of whether it will set us on fire.' Aguek enters a waiting van and drives off, leaving shredded pieces of his passport outside the polling station. Inside, Chol casts his vote and triumphantly holds up his ink-stained finger for the cameras. 'Bye bye, Sharia law; bye bye, slavery,' he says. 'Now (the north) should leave us alone, and we'll leave them alone. We can't be one nation, but we'll be good neighbors.' He makes his way to the waiting vans. In a symbolic act of defiance against the government he wants no part of, he steps over the passport pages scattered outside.
translated_content: Nashville, Tennessee (CNN) -- Moses Chol entra en una camioneta, se frota las manos y hace una señal para que haya silencio. Dirigiéndose a los pasajeros, su rostro se ilumina con una sonrisa, con los dientes brillando a la luz de la mañana. 'Hoy, nos despedimos del norte', anuncia, mientras jóvenes vitorean, visibles a través de bufandas y gorros de lana. Chol se encuentra entre aproximadamente 70 sudaneses del sur reunidos en una fría mañana en el estacionamiento de una iglesia en Clarkston, Georgia, un área metropolitana de Atlanta conocida por su población de refugiados. El grupo viaja a Nashville para votar en un referéndum que podría dividir a Sudán en dos: el norte y el sur. Varios millones de personas en Sudán del Sur están votando esta semana en un referéndum histórico sobre si declarar la independencia del gobierno con sede en Jartum. Alrededor de 55,000 sudaneses del sur están votando en Estados Unidos y otros siete países. Chol encabeza un convoy de más de una docena de automóviles. Al salir del estacionamiento, algunos pasajeros cantan una canción de antiguos guerrilleros que ahora lideran el gobierno y el ejército del Sudán del Sur semiautónomo. 'Nunca nos rendiremos; seguiremos luchando hasta conseguir lo que queremos', cantan en árabe. Al final de la canción, levantan los puños y corean: '¡Sí a la separación!' El referéndum forma parte del Acuerdo General de Paz de 2005, que ayudó a poner fin a dos décadas de guerra civil, con un saldo de aproximadamente 2 millones de muertes. La guerra enfrentó a un gobierno dominado por musulmanes árabes en el norte de Sudán contra cristianos negros o animistas en el sur. Para Chol, el referéndum es casi una reparación. Es uno de los Niños Perdidos, una generación que huyó de la guerra civil y ahora está dispersa por todo el mundo. Estados Unidos reasentó a casi 4,000 de ellos hace una década, aproximadamente. Los hombres, ahora en su mayoría entre los 20 y los 30 años, han pasado la última década reconstruyendo sus vidas. La guerra obligó a Chol y a otros a recorrer cientos de kilómetros a través de desiertos y pantanos, evitando leones y otros animales salvajes, durante su éxodo hacia países vecinos. Una vez allí, vivieron durante años en campos de refugiados. Chol, de 32 años, dice que ha soñado con este referéndum durante mucho tiempo. 'Es hora de que escuchen nuestras voces, de que nos rebelemos contra todo el dolor que hemos sufrido', dice el estudiante de posgrado. 'Mucha gente ha muerto para que llegara este día... No me importa qué gobierno venga después. Ningún gobierno puede ser peor que este'. Su voz se quiebra y se queda mirando al vacío. 'Aprobar este referéndum significa que mi padre no murió en vano. Significa que nuestros hijos no vivirán marcados por el sufrimiento... Seremos los últimos 'Niños Perdidos' que Sudán verá'. El conflicto dejó cicatrices en toda una generación en el remoto Sudán del Sur, que tiene aproximadamente el tamaño de Texas, pero muy pocos caminos pavimentados. A lo largo de los años, cientos de miles de sudaneses huyeron del sur para escapar de los combates y la hambruna. Aproximadamente el 80% de las reservas de petróleo de Sudán se encuentran en el sur, lo que también es fuente de conflictos. Aunque el norte se ha desarrollado más, el sur permanece prácticamente igual, según Chol. 'En el norte dicen que quieren que seamos un solo país', afirma. '¿Cómo podemos serlo si allí tienen escuelas y agua potable, y sus hijos no se mueren de enfermedades que se pueden prevenir? En el sur, la gente todavía bebe agua estancada. No tienen nada'. Otros pasajeros se suman a las quejas contra el norte. Algunos mencionan los intentos del norte de imponer la sharia, o ley islámica, a los no musulmanes, una de las causas principales del estallido de la guerra civil en 1983. La sharia sigue siendo la ley en el norte de Sudán. 'Mira mi pelo. En el norte me metería en problemas por la sharia', dice Grace Ajawin, empleada de una panadería, señalando sus trenzas africanas rojas. 'Quiero que mis hijos puedan salir de casa sin que los obliguen a cubrirse el pelo, a vestirse como quieran, a ir a la iglesia sin que los obliguen a convertirse al islam'. El presidente sudanés, Omar al-Bashir, ha advertido de que endurecerá la aplicación de la sharia en el norte de Sudán si Sudán del Sur vota a favor de la independencia. Todos en las camionetas están convencidos de que el sur se separará del norte. Descartan cualquier otra posibilidad. Le reprenden a Ajawin cuando dice que 'nunca' volverá a Sudán si Al-Bashir no respeta el resultado de la votación a favor de la separación. '¿Cómo no va a respetar (Al-Bashir) el resultado si todo el mundo lo está mirando?', replica Marko Ayii, de 25 años. 'Deja de ser tan negativa'. Chol dice que volverá a su país si Sudán del Sur renace como una nueva nación. 'Cuando me gradúe, les daré las gracias a los estadounidenses por su amabilidad e iré a ayudar a mi gente', declara. Después de unas cuatro horas, el convoy llega al Lost Boys Center, un edificio de ladrillo rojo de una planta situado justo al sur de los rascacielos del centro de Nashville. El centro es uno de los ocho centros de votación que hay en Estados Unidos y que permanecerán abiertos hasta el sábado. Según informan los responsables electorales, más de 900 sudaneses del sur se han registrado para votar allí. Los otros centros están en Boston, Chicago, Dallas, Omaha (Nebraska), Phoenix, Seattle y Washington D.C. La votación está organizada por la Comisión del Referéndum de Sudán del Sur. Frente al centro de Nashville espera una multitud. Algunos bailan y otros ondean banderas de Estados Unidos y de Sudán del Sur. Al frente de la cola, Malual Machop, de 42 años y residente en Nashville, espera su turno para votar, llorando en silencio. 'No lloro de tristeza, sino de alegría', dice. 'Nunca pensé que llegaría a votar por esta separación en mi vida. Hemos sido esclavos durante tanto tiempo. Ahora nos estamos liberando'. Afuera, Ngong Aguek, un músico de 42 años de Sudán del Sur que ha viajado desde Orlando para votar, está rompiendo su pasaporte sudanés. La multitud aplaude y vitorea mientras los trozos de papel vuelan por el aire frío y ventoso. 'Este pasaporte me ha esclavizado durante demasiado tiempo', afirma. 'Me ha tratado como a un ciudadano de segunda, ha destrozado mi dignidad y ha matado y separado a mi familia'. El músico afirma que el gobierno del norte le ha perseguido por criticarlo. 'Pero (la verdad) hay que contarla, aunque nos quememos en el intento'. Aguek sube a una camioneta que lo espera y se aleja, dejando los pedazos de su pasaporte esparcidos frente al centro de votación. Dentro, Chol deposita su voto y levanta triunfalmente el dedo manchado de tinta para que lo fotografíen. '¡Adiós, ley sharia; adiós, esclavitud!', exclama. 'Ahora (el norte) debería dejarnos en paz, y nosotros a ellos. No podemos ser un solo país, pero podemos ser buenos vecinos'. Se dirige hacia las camionetas que lo esperan. En un gesto simbólico de desafío contra el gobierno del que no quiere formar parte, pisa los trozos de pasaporte esparcidos por el suelo.

article_content: The Colombian Football Federation (FCF) has confirmed that Radamel Falcao, Colombia's star striker and a player whose World Cup participation is uncertain due to injury, will join the national team in Buenos Aires as they prepare for the tournament in Brazil. This announcement puts an end to speculation that Falcao would travel to Bogota to declare his withdrawal from the World Cup squad because of his incomplete recovery from knee ligament surgery. According to a statement released by the FCF, 'Radamel Falcao Garcia will be with his teammates in Buenos Aires. Currently, the forward is continuing his rehabilitation at his club, Monaco.' Falcao, aged 28, sustained knee ligament damage while playing for Monaco in a French Cup match in January. He scored nine goals in 13 games during Colombia's South American qualifying campaign, where they finished second to Argentina. The FCF also indicated that the final decision regarding Falcao's inclusion in the World Cup squad – Colombia's first appearance in the tournament in 16 years – will be made by June 2. This is the deadline for Argentine coach Jose Pekerman to announce his 23-man squad. Pekerman had previously included Falcao, known as 'Tigre,' in his provisional 30-man squad the previous week. Before heading to Brazil, Colombia will travel to Argentina next week and play pre-World Cup friendlies against Senegal on May 31 and Jordan on June 6 in Buenos Aires, the hometown of coach Pekerman. At the World Cup, Colombia will compete in Group C, facing Greece, Ivory Coast, and Japan in that order, with the tournament kicking off on June 12. Falcao's presence is considered vital for Colombia, highlighted by his nine goals in 13 qualifying matches.

article_content: A recent study indicates that one in four parents now have at least one adult child residing with them. This situation is largely influenced by elevated property values and substantial rental deposits. The typical cost of homes in some areas of London exceeds £1 million, while national average rents stand at £740 per month. The National Housing Federation reports the 'empty nest syndrome' is becoming less common. Most parents surveyed indicated their children 'simply could not afford independent living'. According to the Office for National Statistics, approximately three million adults aged 20 to 34 are living with their parents, an increase of 20 percent since 1997. Men are more frequently living with parents than women, with figures at 1.8 million and 1.1 million respectively. David Orr states that the traditional 'rite of passage' of moving out is increasingly unattainable due to rising housing costs. The study, which polled 1,176 parents with children aged 21 to 40, found that 27 percent were cohabitating with their adult children. This arrangement can negatively impact parents; 23 percent reported experiencing stress, 18 percent cited family disagreements, and 8 percent faced debt. Craig Berry, 27, lives with his two sisters and their 60-year-old father in Bradford, all striving to save for their own homes. Craig acknowledges the stress his living situation causes his father, especially during arguments. The English Housing Survey reveals homeownership has decreased to levels not seen since the 1980s. Homeownership peaked at 71 percent in 2003 but has since declined to 65.3 percent. Individuals aged 65 and over represent the largest group of homeowners in England, totaling a record 30 percent.

article_content: Tanya Miller, 30, from Carlisle, involved her eight-month-old baby in an armed robbery in Silloth. A mother-of-four has been jailed for acting as the getaway driver in an armed robbery while her eight-month-old baby was with her. Tanya Miller, 30, brought her baby girl in a car seat when she drove from Carlisle to Silloth for the knifepoint robbery at the Cumberland Building Society branch. A judge called it one of the 'most troubling' aspects of the case when Miller appeared in court for her role in the robbery, which traumatized a staff member. Carlisle Crown Court heard that Miller, from Harraby, was the getaway driver while her boyfriend, Barry Doswell, 26, also from Harraby, was 'back-up'. The pair were scheduled for a robbery trial on Wednesday but pleaded guilty before it began. Miller and Doswell were each sentenced to six years in jail for robbery. The court was told that their accomplice, Kevin Docherty, 34, who had no fixed address, entered the building society armed with a knife and stole almost £3,000. Docherty entered the branch in a white jacket, his face mostly covered by a hood, carrying a 12-inch blade. He demanded money from the cashier, threatening to kill her, and she handed over £2,900 in cash before he left the branch. Witnesses saw a blue Ford Focus park in a lane between Station Road and Eden Street. Miller was with her boyfriend, Barry Doswell, who the court heard acted as 'back-up' during the building society raid. A male matching the description exited the vehicle and entered the Building Society. Shortly after, the witness saw the man return to the vehicle, enter the boot, and the vehicle drove off towards Eden Street, with the baby still in the car seat. The April raid led to a large police manhunt involving road blocks and a helicopter, though no one was injured. Judge Paul Batty QC said a female employee at the building society was 'absolutely traumatized' by the raid. The judge also noted that Miller had her eight-month-old child, believed to be Miller and Doswell's daughter, with her. Addressing Doswell and Miller - Docherty was not in court for the hearing - Judge Batty said: 'Each of you played an integral part. Miller was jailed for six years at Carlisle Crown Court after admitting robbery, driving the getaway car with her eight-month-old daughter. Barry Doswell was jailed for six years, and Kevin Docherty was sentenced to seven years in prison. 'A custodial sentence of considerable length is quite inevitable.' Docherty was also sentenced to seven years for robbery and possessing an offensive weapon in a public place. After the sentence, Detective Inspector Ian Harwood said: 'Kevin Docherty subjected the cashiers to a horrendous ordeal while making threats and brandishing a knife. The courts have shown that this behavior will not be tolerated in this county and should serve as a warning to any criminal contemplating such a crime. I’d like to thank the victims and witnesses of the robbery for their bravery and tenacity in helping police put these three in prison. This incident caused great distress to innocent members of the public, and we are happy that justice has been served and these three people are being removed from society.' In the last post on their joint Facebook page, Doswell wrote to Miller: 'My baby, you are so sexy. I am so proud to say you are my wife-to-be. I can't wait to be your husband and make you Mrs. Doswell. You've made me a proud dad and give me 4 beautiful kids. I love them so much, my girl. You mean the world to me, beautiful. Love you millions forever xxx.' To which Miller replied: 'Love you millions baby xx.'

article_content: According to court documents, the Arkansas Supreme Court has ordered the immediate dismissal of Judge Michael Maggio for disclosing confidential information regarding Charlize Theron's adoption case. Judge Maggio of Faulkner County Circuit Court admitted to posting details about Theron's closed adoption record from 2012 on 'tigerdroppings.com,' a Louisiana State University fan site. He used the online alias 'geauxjudge,' according to documents submitted to the state Supreme Court by the Arkansas Judicial Discipline and Disability Commission. In January 2012, Maggio commented that a friend handled Theron's single-parent adoption case and described her appearance in court as wearing 'a long brown wig, oversized clothes' to avoid recognition, as stated in the commission's report. Documents indicate that he also wrote online that he 'offered to be the baby daddy'. Charlize Theron is a prominent Hollywood actress known for her roles in films like 'Monster,' 'Mighty Joe Young,' 'North Country,' and 'Snow White and the Huntsman.' Attempts to contact Theron's representatives for comment were unsuccessful. Maggio's published remarks on the adoption case were part of a report by the Arkansas Judicial Discipline and Disability Commission, which investigated the claims against him. Maggio had served on the bench in Arkansas since 2001. The commission's report included five pages of Maggio's comments under the username 'geauxjudge,' covering various aspects of gender, race, and sexuality issues. The report concluded that he violated at least 23 judicial codes. In March, after his identity as 'geauxjudge' was confirmed, Maggio stated, 'I take full responsibility for the comments that have been attributed to me. I apologize deeply for my lapse in personal judgment, for which I have no excuse.' According to CNN affiliate KATV, the judge's statement continued: 'The comments posted were not acceptable and are not a reflection of who I am.' The Arkansas Supreme Court order prohibits Maggio from holding any judicial office in the state and mandates his removal from office without pay. CNN's Philip Gast and Carolyn Sung contributed to this report.

article_content: A collision between two vessels on the Congo River in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has left as many as 100 individuals unaccounted for, according to the World Health Organization. The incident transpired on Thursday morning, but details have only recently surfaced. Eugene Kabambi, a spokesperson for the WHO in Kinshasa, stated that the accident took place at a location downstream from Kwamouth. An overloaded barge, heading towards Inongo, struck a boat carrying around 150 passengers. 'We are actively searching for potentially 100 missing persons in the Congo River and providing assistance with medical supplies and body bags,' Kabambi mentioned. 'One of the boats was completely destroyed and is believed to be the vessel with the missing people on board.' Kabambi added that the provincial minister of transportation and infrastructure informed his team on Friday that approximately 42 individuals were rescued from the estimated 100 passengers the minister reported. However, based on accounts from survivors, the WHO estimates the number of passengers to be closer to 150. A statement from the WHO released on Friday indicated that three bodies have been recovered from the river. The absence of a passenger manifest makes it challenging to ascertain the exact number of people aboard the privately owned vessel. No injuries were reported on the barge. It is believed that strong currents near the Ngobila rapids caused the accident. The WHO stated that overloaded barges and passenger boats frequently sink in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, specifically on the Congo River and the country's lakes. This is typically attributed to the age of the vessels and the failure to adhere to safe navigation practices; the organization was awaiting delivery of medical supplies and body bags to the affected area on Saturday.

article_content: Jessica Masuglia, now 24, from Melbourne, reflects on a childhood that appeared 'pretty happy' in photos, filled with costumes and birthday celebrations. However, beneath the surface lay the complexities of being raised by a mother, Kim Mackenzie, who struggled with heroin addiction. Kim Mackenzie tragically passed away from an overdose a few years ago at the age of 43, just one week after Jessica's 21st birthday. Despite her mother's addiction, Jessica remembers a loving upbringing. 'Even though my mum was a heroin addict, she was a great mum,' Jessica shared with Daily Mail Australia. Now, Jessica is opening up about hiding her mother's addiction throughout her childhood. Jessica recounts, 'My mum was amazing, full of love and very hands-on. She'd do anything to make me happy.' Kim Mackenzie battled sobriety for much of Jessica's life. While Jessica noticed her mother was different, she didn't grasp the reality of the heroin abuse until she got older. 'For much of my young life, she was straight. She would relapse for a few weeks, then stop. After six months, it would start again,' she explained. 'She was two different people.' Jessica recalls one overdose where her mother had to be revived, but she never witnessed her mother using drugs, believing her mother tried to shield her. The relationship became strained during Jessica's teenage years when her mother developed drug-induced psychosis, also battling alcoholism. 'It was incredibly hard. She had mood swings and would lash out. It hurt to see her struggling with addiction and our constant arguments,' she said. Jessica moved out at 16, and she and her mother were estranged for four years before Kim's death. 'I had expected it for a while, but it was still difficult. I didn't know what to feel. It was the first significant loss in my life,' Jessica confessed. 'Guilt was a dominant emotion because I hadn't seen her. I felt partly responsible, especially since things worsened after our separation.' Looking back, Jessica reflects, 'There were times I didn’t think she was a good mum because I was hurting. But, I now realize how much she loved me.' Kim Mackenzie battled heroin, pills, and later, alcohol throughout her life. Jessica's decision to share her story comes from controversial discussions about drug testing welfare recipients. 'It bothers me when people say drug users waste their dole money on drugs,' she states. 'My mum used her dole money to feed me and provide shelter. The money wasn’t solely for drugs, and that’s not always the case.' Jessica concludes, 'Drug addiction and mental health are still stigmatized because of a lack of understanding. I don't think people will understand until they love someone with an addiction.'
